notes.meaning: God calls Jerusalem to wake up from her long sadness and put on royal, clean robes. Her time of punishment is over, and the Lord is giving her back her dignity and strength. Foreign oppressors who despise God will no longer march in to ruin or defile the holy city.

The captive people are told to stand up out of the dust, which was the traditional place of deep mourning. Instead of lying helpless on the ground like a slave, Jerusalem is invited to take a seat of royal honor. God is removing the heavy chains of bondage from her neck.

Israel was given over to their captors because of their sins, and the conquerors paid nothing to purchase them. Because no price was paid to God for them, God will set them free without paying their enemies any ransom money. To redeem means to buy back and deliver, showing that God frees His people purely by His own grace.

God recalls how His people first went down to Egypt as peaceful guests during a famine, only to be harshly enslaved later on. Afterwards, the Assyrian empire attacked and oppressed them without any fair excuse. Since the Lord rescued Israel from both of those cruel powers, He is just as able to deliver them from Babylon.

The Lord speaks as though asking why He should sit back while His people suffer under proud conquerors for no good reason. The cruel rulers mock Israel and boast as if the God of Israel were powerless to stop them. God will step in to deliver His people for the sake of His own holy name.

When God delivers His captives, they will know by personal experience who their Lord truly is. They will see that every promise He spoke in the past was completely trustworthy. When the day of salvation arrives, God answers their cries by stepping forward and saying, 'Here I am!'

A messenger running over the rugged hills is a beautiful sight because he carries long-awaited news of peace and deliverance. He shouts to the broken city that her God is alive, active, and reigning as King. The New Testament applies this joyful greeting to those who preach the good news of Jesus Christ.

The sentinels standing on the city walls lift up their voices together in a loud shout of joy. They see clearly with their own eyes that the Lord is arriving in person to bring His people home. Their shared song celebrates the unmistakable presence and victory of God.

Even the broken heaps and ruined walls of Jerusalem are called to burst into joyful singing. The Lord has poured out comfort on His grieving people and purchased their freedom. What once looked entirely abandoned and lifeless will now be restored under God's loving care.

God rolls up His sleeves like a warrior stepping onto the battlefield to defend His people. He displays His holy power openly so that all foreign nations can see what He is doing. The rescue of Israel is a living witness pointing toward the salvation God offers to the whole earth.

The captives are urged to pack up and leave Babylon, refusing to take any of its idols or corrupt customs with them. The priests and Levites who carry the sacred temple items back to Jerusalem must keep themselves spiritually pure and clean. God expects those who belong to Him to live holy lives that are set apart from the world.

Unlike the midnight rush when their ancestors escaped from Egypt, this march out of exile will be calm, orderly, and secure. The exiles do not have to sneak away like terrified runaways. The Lord walks in front to guide their way, and He also stands behind them as a rear guard to shield them from danger.

God directs everyone to look upon His Servant, the Messiah, who will act with wisdom and complete His mission successfully. Though He must endure terrible hardship first, He will eventually be raised up and given the highest place of honor. This introduces the famous prophecy of Jesus Christ's suffering and ultimate glory.

Crowds were stunned and horrified when they saw the depths of the Servant's humiliation and abuse. His face and body were bruised and torn so severely that He barely looked like a human being. This pointed directly to the brutal beatings, mocking, and crucifixion that Jesus took upon Himself.

Just as many people were appalled by His suffering, the Servant will sprinkle and purify many nations through His atoning sacrifice. Earthly kings will stand in silent, reverent wonder before Him because they will witness a glorious truth they had never imagined. His work of cleansing from sin reaches far beyond Israel to embrace people from every nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern translators render the Hebrew word as 'startle' rather than 'sprinkle,' meaning the Servant will astonish the nations just as people were previously shocked by His disfigurement.
